“We will, that this body die,

be dissolved, and sink into union
with the Body of Christ at large…”

Last Will and Testament of the Springfield Presbytery, 1804
The cold open. No clicks. Read the first line and stop; let “die” sit before you read on. The sentence goes on: “for there is but one body, and one spirit, even as we are called in one hope of our calling” (Ephesians 4:4).
→ Then last week’s ideas, and then name it: the title.
Last week’s ideas
1.Freedom of conscience is how Christ has built his body.
2.Only Christ can unite us.
3.Christ has already made us one.
4.Our first duty is to recognize it.
Four of last week’s ideas, all at once. Read them, or let the room read them; do not re-teach.
→ “Tonight, five years earlier: men who acted on idea three before Campbell wrote it down.”

How do we claim the unity of the body of Christ?

How do we live that now?

And what does it ask of our conscience?

Two clicks. For them these were not two questions but one. What does unity compel conscience to do: to extend, to give up. → “We’re going to see how far they were willing to take this.”
Our Wild Democracy · Chapter 4

The Last Will
and Testament

Cane Ridge, Kentucky · June 28, 1804
Two documents set the course of our movement: the Declaration and Address (the last few weeks) and this one. This one is five years older. Then the recap: Cane Ridge; Thomas Campbell’s fight for unity, carried from Ireland to America; communion for Christians outside his sect; his trial. Unity and freedom of conscience, all along, as one question.
The frame for the hour is a will-reading: who died, of what, what they left, and to whom.
The hour: the will’s opening 3 · the trial and the garden 10 · the cost 4 · it worked, and the problem 8 · the reading of the will 12 · our table 8 · close 5.

A few years after Cane Ridge…

Kentucky and Ohio · 1803
Setup. Cane Ridge was August 1801; the revival kept spreading, and by 1803 five Presbyterian ministers were preaching in its strain.
Five preachers

“There were at this time five preachers in the Presbyterian connection, who were in the same strain of preaching, and whose doctrine was different from that taught in the Confession of Faith of that body. Their names were, Richard McNemar, John Thompson, John Dunlavy, Robert Marshall, and myself…”

Barton W. Stone, Biography (1847)
• The revival has kept going since Cane Ridge, and Stone is one of five ministers preaching in its strain. The sentence goes on: “the three former lived in Ohio, the two latter in Kentucky.” David Purviance, then a candidate for the ministry, “was of the same faith.”
• → Here is what they preached.
What the five preached

“The distinguishing doctrine preached by us was, that God loved the world — the whole world, and sent his Son to save them… that the gospel was the means of salvation… that God required us to believe in his Son, and had given us sufficient evidence in his Word to produce faith in us… that sinners were capable of understanding and believing this testimony, and of acting upon it by coming to the Saviour and obeying him, and from him obtaining salvation and the Holy Spirit.”

Barton W. Stone, Biography (1847)
• Clipped from the slide: “on condition that they believed in him” (after “save them”); “but that this means would never be effectual to this end, until believed and obeyed by us” (after “the means of salvation”); and “if attended to by us” (after “faith in us”).
• Their distinctive teaching.
• Against Westminster: Christ died for the elect only, and the sinner can do nothing until God first regenerates him. Here: the whole world, and the sinner is able to believe.

“We urged upon the sinner to believe now, and receive salvation… that God was as willing to save them now, as he ever was, or ever would be— that no previous qualification was required, or necessary in order to believe in Jesus, and come to him… that Jesus died for all, and that all things were now ready.”

Barton W. Stone, Biography (1847)
• Clipped from the slide, after “receive salvation”: “that in vain they looked for the Spirit to be given them, while they remained in unbelief — they must believe before the Spirit or salvation would be given them.” And after “come to him”: “that if they were sinners, this was their divine warrant to believe in him, and to come to him for salvation.”
• The same paragraph, continued. “No previous qualification” is the open table again, as doctrine: nothing stands between the sinner and Christ.
• Stone says this is the doctrine of their Apology, and that he later dissented from its account of the Atonement.

“When we began first to preach these things, the people appeared as just awakened from the sleep of ages — they seemed to see for the first time that they were responsible beings…”

Barton W. Stone, Biography (1847)
• The sentence goes on: “and that a refusal to use the means appointed, was a damning sin.”
• → Grandmother: the mining camp, the Church of Christ, agency.
• Then the reaction: “The sticklers for orthodoxy amongst us writhed under these doctrines”; they “painfully saw their Confession of Faith neglected.”
Obey God rather than men

“When we neglected it [the Westminster Confession] and followed the Spirit of God, in his word, our minds were enlightened, and our souls were quickened. But when we compared this light, with the confession, they would not agree. We could not withstand God. We chose to hearken to God, rather than men…”

Springfield Presbytery, Apology (1804)
• Acts 5:29. From the Apology they published the next year, on the Confession; the sentence before: “That book never helped, but hindered our faith.” The sentence ends: “and therefore, have taken our leave of that book.”
• → It flourished, and it drew enough ire that the first one they went after was McNemar.

The Trial

Lexington, September 1803.
The Synod of Kentucky · Lexington, September 1803

Richard McNemar is on trial.

Four other ministers are watching.
They preach what he preaches.
The four: Robert Marshall, John Dunlavy, John Thompson, and Barton Stone, the minister of Cane Ridge. Same machinery as Chapter 2, on the other side of the mountains.
Richard McNemar, 1770–1839

“…first took McNemar through their fiery ordeal, for preaching these anti-calvinistic doctrines.”

Barton W. Stone, Biography (1847)
• McNemar, a revival preacher in Ohio. His crime: preaching what the revival preached, that the gospel offer is open to everyone and anyone may respond. That is not what the Westminster Confession says, and every Presbyterian minister had sworn to the Confession.
• The “ordeal” was his own presbytery, the Washington Presbytery (Stone’s sentence calls it “the Presbytery of Springfield, in Ohio”; the records say Washington, and the name would only confuse here). The Synod of Kentucky censured that presbytery for not dealing with him, and his case came up to the Synod at Lexington, September 1803.

“It was plainly hinted to us, that we would not be forgotten by the Synod.”

Stone, whom the room met at Cane Ridge in Chapter 1. “We waited anxiously for the issue, till we plainly saw it would be adverse to him, and consequently to us all.”
→ So, in a recess of the Synod…
The garden

“In a short recess of Synod, we five withdrew to a private garden, where, after prayer for direction, and a free conversation, with a perfect unanimity we drew up a protest… and a declaration of our independence, and of our withdrawal from their jurisdiction, but not from their communion.”

Barton W. Stone, Biography (1847)
• Five men, a recess, a garden, prayer. “A declaration of our independence”: his words, twenty-seven years after the other one. The protest is dated 10 September 1803.

“This protest we immediately presented to the Synod, through their Moderator — it was altogether unexpected by them, and produced very unpleasant feelings; and a profound silence for a few minutes ensued.”

Barton W. Stone, Biography (1847)
• Let the room have a few seconds of silence of its own.

They did not withdraw communion.

Make the Campbell connection here, out loud. The cue, from the Declaration and Address (1809, Appendix): “no man can relinquish his opinions or practices till once convinced that they are wrong… One thing, however, he may do: when not bound by an express command, he need not impose them upon others, by anywise requiring their approbation.” Luther claimed conscience for himself; Campbell extended it to his brother. The Synod could keep communion on its terms; he only asked to keep it on his.
Exit without excommunication

“We do not desire, nor do we consider ourselves to be separated from the Presbyterian church, as Christians, whether ministers or people; we still wish to continue united to them in the bonds of love: we will admit to communion as formerly, and desire to be admitted. It is not our design to form a party.”

The five, letter to their congregations, September 1803 · in Stone, Biography (1847)
• Their circular letter, written right after the protest. They withdrew from the Synod’s jurisdiction, and in the same breath kept the table open both ways: they would still give communion to the men putting them out, and still ask to receive it from them.
• → They left the court. They did not leave the table.
Quoting the Confession against itself

“…we plead a privilege, which is granted in the Confession of Faith, chap. 1. sec. 9, 10… that the infallible rule of interpreting Scripture, is not the Confession of Faith, nor any human writings whatever, but the Scripture itself.”

The five, letter to their congregations, September 1803 · in Stone, Biography (1847)
• Their circular letter, drafted at the new presbytery’s first meeting and signed by all five; it says the protest made the same plea. “We wish to pay all due deference to the Confession of Faith, and other writings of our pious fathers; but…”
• The same letter: “We do not desire, nor do we consider ourselves to be separated from the Presbyterian church… we will admit to communion as formerly, and desire to be admitted. It is not our design to form a party.”
• → The book they were tried by says it is not the final word. Next slide: what it actually says.
Westminster Confession, 1646 · chapter 1
1.9 “The infallible rule of interpretation of Scripture, is the Scripture itself…”
1.10 “The supreme Judge, by which all controversies of religion are to be determined, and all decrees of councils… are to be examined… can be no other but the Holy Spirit speaking in the Scripture.”
Two clicks. The Synod tried them by the Confession; the Confession says every council’s decree is to be examined by Scripture, and the only supreme judge is the Spirit speaking in Scripture. That includes the Synod, and the Confession itself. (Text as in the 1646 Confession; 1.9 goes on: “when there is a question about the true and full sense of any scripture… it [must] be searched and known by other places that speak more clearly.”)
→ They did not reject the Confession. They took it at its word. And the same book says more.
The same Confession
20.2 “God alone is Lord of the conscience, and hath left it free from the doctrines and commandments of men…”
31.3 “All synods or councils since the apostles’ times, whether general or particular, may err, and many have erred; therefore they are not to be made the rule of faith or practice…”
Two clicks. Chapter 20, Of Christian Liberty and Liberty of Conscience; chapter 31, Of Synods and Councils (31.3 in the American text the Synod used; 31.4 in the 1646 original). 20.2 goes on: “the requiring an implicit faith, and an absolute and blind obedience, is to destroy liberty of conscience, and reason also.” 31.3 ends: “but to be used as a help in both.”
→ The Synod of Kentucky was a synod. By its own Confession, it may err.

These men were radical.
But they were also faithful.

Radical in what they did: walked out of a synod, tore up a salary, dissolved their own presbytery. Faithful in why.

They were not breaking with their tradition.
They were honoring its deepest impulses.

Scripture as the only infallible rule; God alone Lord of the conscience; councils may err. Every one is in the Westminster Confession. The Reformation’s own principles, taken seriously: Luther at Worms, again. → And they pressed them further than the Synod would.
The Synod sends a committee to win them back

One of the committee, Matthew Houston, “became convinced that the doctrine we preached was true, and soon after united with us.”

Barton W. Stone, Biography (1847)
A smile. The committee sent to bring them back lost a member to them.
David Rice
“Another of the committee, old father David Rice, of precious memory, on whose influence the Synod chiefly depended to reclaim us, urged one argument worthy of record, it was this — that every departure from Calvinism was an advance to atheism.”
Calvinism → Arminianism → Pelagianism → deism → atheism
Barton W. Stone, Biography (1847)
One click. Rice was the father of Kentucky Presbyterianism, and Stone still honors him; but his argument, Stone says, “could have no effect on minds ardent in the search of truth.” The logic: the creed is the only thing between you and atheism. Last week answered that.
→ Then the Synod suspended them anyway, and sent committees to read “the Synod’s bull of suspension” in their pulpits and declare their churches vacant.
Cane Ridge and Concord · late 1803

“I called together my congregations, and informed them that I could no longer conscientiously preach to support the Presbyterian church… that I absolved them from all obligations in a pecuniary point of view, and then in their presence tore up their salary obligation to me…”

Barton W. Stone, Biography (1847)
• Mime it if you like. He kept preaching to them, “but not in the relation that had previously existed between us.” Of the people: “Never have I found a more loving, kind, and orderly people in any country.” Of the day: “This was truly a day of sorrow, and the impressions of it are indelible.”

“I preferred honesty and a good conscience to all these things. Having now no support from the congregations, and having emancipated my slaves, I turned my attention cheerfully, though awkwardly, to labor on my little farm… often on my return home, I found the weeds were getting ahead of my corn.”

Barton W. Stone, Biography (1847)
• He had already freed the people he had enslaved. Now no salary either. He preached almost every night and worked the field at night “while others were asleep.”
• → And here is the surprise: they flourished.

The Rise of the Springfield Presbytery

Late 1803 to 1804.
They form the Springfield Presbytery and publish the Apology.
The Apology “was quickly republished by the Methodists in Virginia…”
Pamphlets against them, “full of misrepresentation and invective,” spread their views.
People “disgusted and offended” by the attacks “were driven from them, and cleaved to us.”
Barton W. Stone, Biography (1847)
Three clicks. The Methodists reprinted it “except our remarks upon creeds.” Stone: “This book produced a great effect in the Christian community.”

The Springfield Presbytery
flourished.

Churches planted, preachers multiplied. → At their last meeting, they set out to write a book on church government.
Writing a book on church government

“…Observations on Church Government, in which the world will see the beautiful simplicity of Christian church government, stript of human inventions and lordly traditions.”

The Witnesses’ Address, appended to the Last Will and Testament, 1804
• What they found was not only an absence. The authority Christ gave belongs to the gathered church; the will says so: “native right of internal government”, “Christ speaking in them.” Your reading, and say it as yours: Matthew 18:20, where two or three are gathered (next week’s title); every believer a priest. Every other institution answers to that.
• At their last meeting they set out to write Observations on Church Government. The next sentence: “As they proceeded in the investigation of that subject, they soon found that there was neither precept nor example in the New Testament for such confederacies as modern Church Sessions, Presbyteries, Synods, General Assemblies, etc.” The research convicted the researchers: their own presbytery was one of these confederacies. “While they continued in the connection in which they then stood, they were off the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets.” (The book never appeared.)
Why they did it

“…they endeavored to cultivate a spirit of love and unity with all Christians; but found it extremely difficult to suppress the idea that they themselves were a party separate from others. This difficulty increased in proportion to their success in the ministry. Jealousies were excited in the minds of other denominations…”

The Witnesses’ Address, appended to the Last Will and Testament, 1804
• The witnesses who signed the will, explaining it. They left a party because it fenced Christians apart. Now people saw them as a party, and they began to feel like one. Stone: “we had not worn our name more than one year, before we saw it savored of a party spirit.”

Success was making them
the thing they had protested.

Say it once. Failure would have been easy to read; success was the danger.

They caught their own presbytery
being handed a job only Christ can do.

Last week’s thesis, lived five years before it was written: anything asked to do a job only Christ can do will fail. They did not wait for it to fail.
Why

“Therefore, from a principle of love to Christians of every name, the precious cause of Jesus, and dying sinners who are kept from the Lord by the existence of sects and parties in the church, they have cheerfully consented to retire from the din and fury of conflicting parties — sink out of the view of fleshly minds, and die the death.”

The Witnesses’ Address, appended to the Last Will and Testament, 1804
• The three reasons: love of Christians of every name; the cause of Jesus; and the people outside, kept from the Lord by our divisions. → So they wrote their will.

The Last Will & Testament

Cane Ridge, June 28, 1804.
Cane Ridge Meeting House · HABS, Theodore Webb, 1934
Cane Ridge · June 28, 1804

The reading of the will.

Back to the room of Chapter 1. Three years earlier, thousands came through the mud to an open table here. The will is dated “sitting at Cane Ridge,” by tradition in this meetinghouse. Signed by six: the five from the garden and David Purviance.
At the top of the page

“For where a testament is, there must of necessity be the death of the testator… Verily, verily I say unto you, except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone; but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.”

The will’s epigraph · Hebrews 9:16; John 12:24
• They put the theology at the top. A will has no force while the testator lives. The inheritance can only pass when the presbytery is gone.
June 28, 1804

“The Presbytery of Springfield, sitting at Cane Ridge… being, through a gracious Providence, in more than ordinary bodily health, growing in strength and size daily, and in perfect soundness and composure of mind; but knowing that it is appointed for all delegated bodies once to die… do make and ordain this our Last Will and Testament…”

Last Will and Testament of the Springfield Presbytery, 1804
• The will’s opening, in the legal form of a real will. Read it slowly; the joke is in “more than ordinary bodily health.” Nobody makes a will because they are growing in strength and size daily.
• → This church body was nine months old, and thriving.

“…it is appointed for
all delegated bodies
once to die.”

Last Will and Testament of the Springfield Presbytery, 1804
From the preamble, after “more than ordinary bodily health.” Hebrews 9:27, “it is appointed unto men once to die,” applied to institutions. Every presbytery, synod, board and program is a delegated body: it holds authority on loan. It is mortal by design.
First bequest

“We will, that this body die, be dissolved, and sink into union with the Body of Christ at large; for there is but one body, and one spirit, even as we are called in one hope of our calling.”

Last Will and Testament of the Springfield Presbytery, 1804
• The line we opened with; now the room knows how they got here. In the will it opens with “Imprimis”: in the first place, the legal word. Ephesians 4:4. The presbytery does not dissolve into nothing; it sinks into the whole church. The heir is the Body of Christ at large.
Their name

“We will, that our name of distinction, with its Reverend title, be forgotten, that there be but one Lord over God’s heritage, and his name one.”

Last Will and Testament of the Springfield Presbytery, 1804
• A will gives things away; this one gives away everything a church body has, starting with its name and its titles. They took the name Christian (Rice Haggard’s pamphlet).
Their power

“We will, that our power of making laws for the government of the church, and executing them by delegated authority, forever cease; that the people may have free course to the Bible, and adopt the law of the spirit of life in Christ Jesus.”

Last Will and Testament of the Springfield Presbytery, 1804
• Not abolished: bequeathed. The power to make law for the church goes back to where they think it belongs.
To the ministers

“We will, that candidates for the Gospel ministry henceforth study the holy scriptures with fervent prayer, and obtain license from God to preach the simple Gospel, with the Holy Ghost sent down from heaven, without any mixture of philosophy, vain deceit, traditions of men, or the rudiments of the world.”

Last Will and Testament of the Springfield Presbytery, 1804
• No presbytery to license a preacher now. The license comes from God, and the Spirit is the credential.
To the church

“We will, that the church of Christ assume her native right of internal government… and admit no other proof of their authority, but Christ speaking in them.”

Last Will and Testament of the Springfield Presbytery, 1804
• “Native”: it was always hers. The church will “try her candidates for the ministry, as to their soundness in the faith, acquaintance with experimental religion, gravity and aptness to teach.” What the Synod did to McNemar, the congregation now does, and the only credential is “Christ speaking in them.”
To every congregation

“We will, that each particular church, as a body, actuated by the same spirit, choose her own preacher, and support him by a free will offering… admit members — remove offences; and never henceforth delegate her right of government to any man or set of men whatever.”

Last Will and Testament of the Springfield Presbytery, 1804
• The biggest bequest. Everything the Synod did to them (try preachers, admit, exclude) is handed to the congregation. The priesthood of all believers, as polity.
• → Hold this one. Next week, at Brush Run, a congregation will use exactly this right.
To preachers and people

“We will, that preachers and people, cultivate a spirit of mutual forbearance; pray more and dispute less; and while they behold the signs of the times, look up, and confidently expect that redemption draweth nigh.”

Last Will and Testament of the Springfield Presbytery, 1804
• A church that has given away its courts has nothing left to settle its quarrels but forbearance and prayer, and the will says so in the same breath. Then: look up; redemption draweth nigh. They died expecting the future.
Their weak brethren

“We will, that our weak brethren, who may have been wishing to make the Presbytery of Springfield their king, and wot not what is now become of it, betake themselves to the Rock of Ages, and follow Jesus for the future.”

Last Will and Testament of the Springfield Presbytery, 1804
• Their own people. Gentle, and a little funny: “wot not what is now become of it.” The presbytery was being asked to stand where Christ stands.
The witnesses to the will

“…from its first existence it [the Springfield Presbytery] was knit together in love, lived in peace and concord, and died a voluntary and happy death.”

The Witnesses’ Address, appended to the Last Will and Testament, 1804
• Not a split, not a failure, not a scandal. A happy death.
The last words

“We heartily unite with our Christian brethren of every name, in thanksgiving to God for the display of his goodness in the glorious work he is carrying on… which we hope will terminate in the universal spread of the Gospel, and the unity of the church.”

The Witnesses’ Address, appended to the Last Will and Testament, 1804
• The closing sentence of the whole pamphlet, just before “The End.” The cut is “in our Western country.” Cane Ridge is still the background: the glorious work is the revival.
After the will

“Having divested ourselves of all party creeds, and party names, and trusting alone in God, and the word of his grace, we became a by-word and laughing stock to the sects around; all prophesying our speedy annihilation. Yet from this period I date the commencement of that reformation, which has progressed to this day.”

Barton W. Stone, Biography (1847)
• “Party names” is the name Springfield Presbytery. Just before this: “we had not worn our name more than one year, before we saw it savored of a party spirit. With the man-made creeds we threw it overboard, and took the name Christian.”
• Stone does not date the movement from Cane Ridge in 1801, or from the garden in 1803. He dates it from here: the giving up of the party.

A will only takes effect
when someone dies.
The heir was the whole church of Christ.

Let it sit before the room.
Our table

What in our church is “in more than ordinary bodily health”?

Would we be willing to let it die?
Discussion, eight minutes. Not what is failing: what is thriving. A program, a name, a building, a way of doing things, a reputation. Which of them is starting to stand where only Christ should stand? Leave it open.
Black.
◆ for discussion

What is beautiful here? What do we carry forward?

Backup prompts (off the slide): What do we keep alive mostly because it is ours? Who in our congregation holds authority that belongs to the gathered church? If our own church were thriving, could we let some part of it die for the sake of unity?
If the room is slow: “What would you put in our will?”
Idea 1 of 3

Unity:
institutional self-sacrifice.

Not just rejecting other religious authorities for the sake of unity, but dissolving even their own: “We will, that this body die, be dissolved, and sink into union with the Body of Christ at large.” The presbytery was thriving, and they let it die.
Idea 2 of 3

Freedom of conscience:
claimed for ourselves, extended to others.

Claimed: “We chose to hearken to God, rather than men.” Paid for: Stone tears up his salary obligation in front of his congregations, and goes back to the farm. Extended: they would not excommunicate their judges: “we will admit to communion as formerly, and desire to be admitted.” Campbell, five years later, the same.
Idea 3 of 3

Priesthood:
authority belongs to gathered believers.

Each church, “actuated by the same spirit,” to “choose her own preacher… admit members… remove offences; and never henceforth delegate her right of government to any man or set of men whatever.” No proof of a minister’s authority “but Christ speaking in them.” → Next week, at Brush Run, a congregation uses exactly this right.
Ideas
1.Unity: institutional self-sacrifice.
2.Freedom of conscience: claimed for ourselves, extended to others.
3.Priesthood: authority belongs to gathered believers.
All three at once, before the discussion.

Addendum

Reference material; not part of the telling.
What they left
Their name, and the Reverend title: “be forgotten, that there be but one Lord over God’s heritage, and his name one.”
Their power of making laws for the church: “forever cease; that the people may have free course to the Bible.”
To the people: “the Bible as the only sure guide to heaven.”
Last Will and Testament of the Springfield Presbytery, 1804
The bequests in one list (the telling gives each its own slide). On the Bible item, the joke: those offended by other books “may cast them into the fire if they choose: for it is better to enter into life having one book, than having many to be cast into hell.”
